claim: Axonal microtubules are organized with the plus-end oriented out from the cell body.
source: Whereas axonal MTs are organized such that the plus-end is oriented out from the cell body, dendrites exhibit a mixed MTs polarity containing both minus-end-out and plus-end-out MTs.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known characteristic of axonal MT organization.

claim: Dendrites exhibit a mixed microtubule polarity containing both minus-end-out and plus-end-out microtubules.
source: Whereas axonal MTs are organized such that the plus-end is oriented out from the cell body, dendrites exhibit a mixed MTs polarity containing both minus-end-out and plus-end-out MTs.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known characteristic of dendritic MT organization.

claim: Kinesin-1 is critical in establishing the characteristic minus-end-out microtubule organization of the dendrite in vivo.
source: Here, we show that kinesin-1 is critical in establishing the characteristic minus-end-out MT organization of the dendrite in vivo.
evidence: This is the primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: In unc-116 (kinesin-1/kinesin heavy chain) mutants, the dendritic microtubules adopt an axonal-like plus-end-out organization.
source: In unc-116 (kinesin-1/kinesin heavy chain) mutants, the dendritic MTs adopt an axonal-like plus-end-out organization.
evidence: This is a key experimental finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated with multiple markers in the results section.

claim: Kinesin-1 protein is able to cross-link anti-paralleled microtubules in vitro.
source: Kinesin-1 protein is able to cross-link anti-paralleled MTs in vitro.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by electron microscopy data in Figure 5.

claim: Kinesin-1 regulates dendrite microtubule polarity through directly gliding the plus-end-out microtubules out of the dendrite using both the motor domain and the C-terminal microtubule-binding domain.
source: We propose that kinesin-1 regulates the dendrite MT polarity through directly gliding the plus-end-out MTs out of the dendrite using both the motor domain and the C-terminal MT-binding domain.
evidence: This is the proposed mechanism stated in the abstract and supported by structure-function analyses and in vitro data.

claim: Microtubules are uniformly polarized with their plus-ends oriented toward the distal tip in axons from worm to rodents.
source: Based on the behavior of EB1 in neurites, it was cohesively concluded that MTs are uniformly polarized with their plus-ends oriented toward the distal tip in axons from worm to rodents.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous studies using EB1 imaging.

claim: In cultured vertebrate neurons, microtubules are mixed in the proximal region of dendrites and uniformly plus-end-out in distal parts.
source: In the dendrites, MTs are mixed in the proximal region and uniformly plus-end-out in distal parts in cultured vertebrate neurons, whereas MTs exhibit a mixed orientation with minus-ends predominantly facing the distal dendrite in worm and fly (Baas et al., 1987; Baas et al., 1988; Stepanova et al., 2003; Rolls et al., 2007; Stone et al., 2008; Kollins et al., 2009; Kapitein and Hoogenraad, 2011; Maniar et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous studies cited in the text.

claim: In worm and fly dendrites, microtubules exhibit a mixed orientation with minus-ends predominantly facing the distal dendrite.
source: In the dendrites, MTs are mixed in the proximal region and uniformly plus-end-out in distal parts in cultured vertebrate neurons, whereas MTs exhibit a mixed orientation with minus-ends predominantly facing the distal dendrite in worm and fly (Baas et al., 1987; Baas et al., 1988; Stepanova et al., 2003; Rolls et al., 2007; Stone et al., 2008; Kollins et al., 2009; Kapitein and Hoogenraad, 2011; Maniar et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous studies cited in the text.

claim: YFP-tagged UNC-104/Kinesin3 exhibits dim diffuse fluorescence along the axon with dramatic accumulation at the distal tip in DA9 neurons.
source: We found that YFP-tagged UNC-104/Kinesin3 exhibits dim diffuse fluorescence along the axon with dramatic accumulation at the distal tip, but is completely absent from the dendrite (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: YFP-tagged UNC-104/Kinesin3 is completely absent from the dendrite in wild-type DA9 neurons.
source: We found that YFP-tagged UNC-104/Kinesin3 exhibits dim diffuse fluorescence along the axon with dramatic accumulation at the distal tip, but is completely absent from the dendrite (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: DHC-1/dynein heavy chain fused with GFP shows weak staining along the dendrite with accumulation at the distal tip of the dendrite in DA9 neurons.
source: Conversely, DHC-1/dynein heavy chain fused with GFP shows weak staining along the dendrite with accumulation at the distal tip of the dendrite (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation stated in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: GFP fused to the slow Ncd family minus-end kinesin, KLP-16, exhibits a graded fluorescence signal from proximal to distal dendrite with accumulation at the distal tip of the dendrite in DA9 neurons.
source: In addition, GFP fused to the slow Ncd family minus-end kinesin, KLP-16, exhibits a graded fluorescence signal from proximal to distal dendrite with accumulation at the distal tip of the dendrite (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is an experimental observation stated in the text and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The specific localization of the tagged KLP-16 motor is dependent on its motor activity.
source: The specific localization of the tagged KLP-16 motor is dependent on its motor activity, as motor-dead versions are largely diffuse through the DA9 processes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an experimental observation stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Motor-dead versions of KLP-16 are largely diffuse through the DA9 processes.
source: The specific localization of the tagged KLP-16 motor is dependent on its motor activity, as motor-dead versions are largely diffuse through the DA9 processes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an experimental observation stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Microtubules are uniformly plus-end-out in the axon of C. elegans DA9 neurons.
source: These localization data are consistent with previous observations made in mammalian and Drosophila neurons, which suggest that MTs are uniformly plus-end-out in the axon and predominantly minus-end-out in the dendrite.
evidence: This is inferred from the localization patterns of motor proteins and consistent with previous observations.

claim: Microtubules are predominantly minus-end-out in the dendrite of C. elegans DA9 neurons.
source: These localization data are consistent with previous observations made in mammalian and Drosophila neurons, which suggest that MTs are uniformly plus-end-out in the axon and predominantly minus-end-out in the dendrite.
evidence: This is inferred from the localization patterns of motor proteins and consistent with previous observations.

claim: The majority of the EBP-2::GFP comets in the axon move away from soma in wild-type DA9 and PHC neurons.
source: The majority of the EBP-2::GFP comets in the axon move away from soma, whereas the majority of comets in the dendrite move toward the soma (Figure 2A–D and Videos 1–3).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from time-lapse imaging stated in the text and shown in Figure 2 and Videos 1-3.

claim: The majority of EBP-2::GFP comets in the dendrite move toward the soma in wild-type DA9 and PHC neurons.
source: The majority of the EBP-2::GFP comets in the axon move away from soma, whereas the majority of comets in the dendrite move toward the soma (Figure 2A–D and Videos 1–3).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from time-lapse imaging stated in the text and shown in Figure 2 and Videos 1-3.

claim: Axonal microtubules are predominantly plus-end-out in wild-type C. elegans neurons.
source: Consistent with published results (Maniar et al., 2012), these data show that axonal MTs are predominantly plus-end-out and dendritic MTs are largely minus-end-out in wild-type C. elegans neurons.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the EBP-2::GFP comet data and consistent with published results.

claim: Dendritic microtubules are largely minus-end-out in wild-type C. elegans neurons.
source: Consistent with published results (Maniar et al., 2012), these data show that axonal MTs are predominantly plus-end-out and dendritic MTs are largely minus-end-out in wild-type C. elegans neurons.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the EBP-2::GFP comet data and consistent with published results.

claim: In unc-116(e2310) mutants, UNC-104::YFP accumulates in the tip of dendrite in addition to its normal localization at the axonal tip.
source: In unc-116(e2310) mutants, UNC-104::YFP also accumulates in the tip of dendrite in addition to its normal localization at the axonal tip (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is an experimental observation stated in the text and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: In unc-116 mutants, the fluorescence signals of DHC-1::GFP and KLP-16::YFP no longer accumulate at the dendrite tip.
source: Furthermore, the fluorescence signals of DHC-1::GFP and KLP-16::YFP no longer accumulate at the dendrite tip; instead, fluorescence is visible only at the dendritic segment nearest the cell body (Figure 1F,G,M).
evidence: This is an experimental observation stated in the text and shown in Figure 1F, G, M.

claim: In unc-116 mutants, DHC-1::GFP and KLP-16::YFP fluorescence is visible only at the dendritic segment nearest the cell body.
source: Furthermore, the fluorescence signals of DHC-1::GFP and KLP-16::YFP no longer accumulate at the dendrite tip; instead, fluorescence is visible only at the dendritic segment nearest the cell body (Figure 1F,G,M).
evidence: This is an experimental observation stated in the text and shown in Figure 1F, G, M.

claim: The changes in the distribution of microtubule polarity markers in unc-116 mutants suggest that dendritic microtubule organization has changed to an axon-like plus-end-out pattern.
source: These changes in the distribution of MT polarity markers suggest that dendritic MT organization has changed to an axon-like plus-end-out pattern in the unc-116 mutants.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental observations of motor protein localization changes.

claim: In unc-116 mutants, dynamic microtubules in the dendrites of both DA9 and PHC neurons almost completely change their behaviors, adopting a predominantly plus-end-out movement.
source: Consistently, in the same mutant dynamic MTs in the dendrites of both DA9 and PHC neurons almost completely change their behaviors, adopting a predominantly plus-end-out movement (Figure 2A–C and Videos 4 and 5).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from time-lapse imaging stated in the text and shown in Figure 2 and Videos 4-5.

claim: The unc-116/kinesin-1 mutation causes microtubule polarity in dendrites to become axon-like, but with no effect on microtubule orientation in the axon.
source: These data further indicate that the unc-116/kinesin-1 mutation causes MT polarity in dendrites to become axon-like, but with no effect on MT orientation in the axon.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the EBP-2::GFP comet data in unc-116 mutants.

claim: UNC-116 encodes the sole C. elegans ortholog of kinesin-1.
source: UNC-116 encodes the sole C. elegans ortholog of kinesin-1 (previously called kinesin heavy chain or KHC) (Siddiqui, 2002).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: Complete loss of unc-116 leads to embryonic lethality.
source: Since complete loss of unc-116 leads to embryonic lethality and unc-116(e2310) is viable, the e2310 allele likely represents a partial loss-of-function mutant.
evidence: This is stated as known information about the unc-116 gene.

claim: unc-116(e2310) is viable.
source: Since complete loss of unc-116 leads to embryonic lethality and unc-116(e2310) is viable, the e2310 allele likely represents a partial loss-of-function mutant.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about the e2310 allele.

claim: The e2310 allele likely represents a partial loss-of-function mutant.
source: Since complete loss of unc-116 leads to embryonic lethality and unc-116(e2310) is viable, the e2310 allele likely represents a partial loss-of-function mutant.
evidence: This is inferred from the viability of e2310 compared to complete loss-of-function.

claim: Two additional partial loss-of-function alleles of unc-116, wy270 and rh24sb79, show similar mislocalization of microtubule motors in the DA9 dendrite.
source: Two additional partial loss-of-function alleles of unc-116, wy270 and rh24sb79, show similar mislocalization of MT motors in the DA9 dendrite, suggesting that this phenotype is indeed due to loss of the protein activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an experimental observation stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cell autonomous expression of wild-type UNC-116 in unc-116(e2310) mutants rescued the dendritic distribution phenotype of KLP-16.
source: Consistent with this notion, cell autonomous expression of wild-type UNC-116 in unc-116(e2310) mutants rescued the dendritic distribution phenotype of KLP-16, indicating that UNC-116 functions in the DA9 neuron (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from a rescue experiment stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: UNC-116 functions in the DA9 neuron.
source: Consistent with this notion, cell autonomous expression of wild-type UNC-116 in unc-116(e2310) mutants rescued the dendritic distribution phenotype of KLP-16, indicating that UNC-116 functions in the DA9 neuron (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is concluded from the cell-autonomous rescue experiment.

claim: UNC-116's function is required for establishing the minus-end-out microtubule organization in the dendrite.
source: Taken together, these data support the idea that UNC-116's function is required for establishing the minus-end-out MT organization in the dendrite.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutant phenotypes and rescue experiments.

claim: In wild-type animals, DA9 axonal outgrowth and neuromuscular junction formation occur embryonically.
source: In wild-type animals, DA9 axonal outgrowth and neuromuscular junction formation occur embryonically, whereas most dendrite outgrowth takes place postembryonically starting from the L1 stage (Teichmann and Shen, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as known information about DA9 development with a citation.

claim: Most dendrite outgrowth in DA9 takes place postembryonically starting from the L1 stage.
source: In wild-type animals, DA9 axonal outgrowth and neuromuscular junction formation occur embryonically, whereas most dendrite outgrowth takes place postembryonically starting from the L1 stage (Teichmann and Shen, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as known information about DA9 development with a citation.

claim: In the unc-116(e2310) mutants, the sequence and directionality of axonal and dendrite outgrowth are indistinguishable from that of the wild-type strain.
source: In the unc-116(e2310) mutants, the sequence and directionality of axonal and dendrite outgrowth as well as the length of the axon are indistinguishable from that of the wild-type strain.
evidence: This is an experimental observation comparing unc-116 mutants to wild-type.

claim: In the unc-116(e2310) mutants, the length of the axon is indistinguishable from that of the wild-type strain.
source: In the unc-116(e2310) mutants, the sequence and directionality of axonal and dendrite outgrowth as well as the length of the axon are indistinguishable from that of the wild-type strain.
evidence: This is an experimental observation comparing unc-116 mutants to wild-type.

claim: The length of the DA9 dendrite is dramatically longer compared with wild-type animals at every stage of development in unc-116(e2310) mutants.
source: The length of the DA9 dendrite, however, is dramatically longer compared with wild-type animals at every stage of development (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an experimental observation stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The UNC-104/Imac/kinesin3 motor traffics synaptic vesicles to presynaptic specializations.
source: The UNC-104/Imac/kinesin3 motor traffics SVs to presynaptic specializations (Hall and Hedgecock, 1991), and synaptic vesicle proteins like RAB-3 exclusively accumulate in the axon of wild-type animals (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated as known information with a citation.

claim: Synaptic vesicle proteins like RAB-3 exclusively accumulate in the axon of wild-type animals.
source: The UNC-104/Imac/kinesin3 motor traffics SVs to presynaptic specializations (Hall and Hedgecock, 1991), and synaptic vesicle proteins like RAB-3 exclusively accumulate in the axon of wild-type animals (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation stated in the text and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In unc-104(e1265) mutants, synaptic vesicle markers are completely absent from the axon.
source: In unc-104(e1265) mutants, SV markers are completely absent from the axon, accumulating instead in the cell body and dendrite due to the activity of dynein (Figure 3C; Ou et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an experimental observation stated in the text and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In unc-104(e1265) mutants, synaptic vesicle markers accumulate in the cell body and dendrite due to the activity of dynein.
source: In unc-104(e1265) mutants, SV markers are completely absent from the axon, accumulating instead in the cell body and dendrite due to the activity of dynein (Figure 3C; Ou et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an experimental observation stated in the text and shown in Figure 3C, with a citation supporting the dynein mechanism.

claim: In unc-116(e2310) mutants, both the axon and dendrite contain a similar number of vesicle clusters.
source: Interestingly, we found that in unc-116(e2310) mutants, both the axon and dendrite contain a similar number of vesicle clusters (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an experimental observation stated in the text and shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: In unc-104(e1265);unc-116(e2310) double mutants, synaptic vesicles are largely absent from both processes and trapped in the cell body.
source: Indeed, in unc-104(e1265);unc-116(e2310) double mutants, SVs are largely absent from both processes and trapped in the cell body.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from a double mutant analysis.

claim: UNC-116 is not directly involved in synaptic vesicle transport in the DA9 neuron.
source: These results argue that UNC-116 is not directly involved in SV transport in the DA9 neuron; rather, it creates the minus-end-out MT polarity of the dendrite.
evidence: This is concluded from the double mutant analysis showing that SV accumulation in dendrites depends on UNC-104.

claim: UNC-116 creates the minus-end-out microtubule polarity of the dendrite.
source: These results argue that UNC-116 is not directly involved in SV transport in the DA9 neuron; rather, it creates the minus-end-out MT polarity of the dendrite.
evidence: This is concluded from the genetic analysis showing that SV mislocalization is secondary to MT polarity changes.

claim: As a result of aberrant microtubule polarity in unc-116 mutants, the plus-end motor UNC-104 promotes locomotion of cargoes into the dendrite.
source: As a result of this aberrant MT polarity, the plus-end motor UNC-104 promotes locomotion of cargoes into the dendrite.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic epistasis analysis showing UNC-104 is required for SV accumulation in dendrites of unc-116 mutants.

claim: The active zone protein SYD-2/liprin shows ectopic localization to DA9 dendrites in the unc-116(e2310) mutants.
source: Indeed, the active zone protein SYD-2/liprin and other SV markers like SNG-1/synaptogyrin show similar ectopic localization to DA9 dendrites in the unc-116(e2310) mutants, suggesting that the changes in MT polarity affect the entire presynaptic structure (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an experimental observation stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Other synaptic vesicle markers like SNG-1/synaptogyrin show similar ectopic localization to DA9 dendrites in the unc-116(e2310) mutants.
source: Indeed, the active zone protein SYD-2/liprin and other SV markers like SNG-1/synaptogyrin show similar ectopic localization to DA9 dendrites in the unc-116(e2310) mutants, suggesting that the changes in MT polarity affect the entire presynaptic structure (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an experimental observation stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The changes in microtubule polarity affect the entire presynaptic structure.
source: Indeed, the active zone protein SYD-2/liprin and other SV markers like SNG-1/synaptogyrin show similar ectopic localization to DA9 dendrites in the unc-116(e2310) mutants, suggesting that the changes in MT polarity affect the entire presynaptic structure (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that multiple presynaptic proteins mislocalize to dendrites in unc-116 mutants.

claim: An acetylcholine receptor (ACR-2) is dendritically enriched in DA9.
source: An acetylcholine receptor (ACR-2), a receptor tyrosine kinase (CAM-1), and a gap junction protein (FBN-1) are all reported to be dendritically enriched in DA9 (Sieburth et al., 2005; Barbagallo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as known information with citations.

claim: A receptor tyrosine kinase (CAM-1) is dendritically enriched in DA9.
source: An acetylcholine receptor (ACR-2), a receptor tyrosine kinase (CAM-1), and a gap junction protein (FBN-1) are all reported to be dendritically enriched in DA9 (Sieburth et al., 2005; Barbagallo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as known information with citations.

claim: A gap junction protein (FBN-1) is dendritically enriched in DA9.
source: An acetylcholine receptor (ACR-2), a receptor tyrosine kinase (CAM-1), and a gap junction protein (FBN-1) are all reported to be dendritically enriched in DA9 (Sieburth et al., 2005; Barbagallo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as known information with citations.

claim: In wild-type DA9 neurons, fluorescently tagged ACR-2, CAM-1, and FBN-1 all localize to the dendrite, cell body, and the initial part of the ventral axon.
source: In wild-type DA9 neurons, fluorescently tagged ACR-2, CAM-1, and FBN-1 all localize to the dendrite, cell body, and the initial part of the ventral axon.
evidence: This is an experimental observation of protein localization in wild-type neurons.

claim: In unc-116(e2310) animals, dendritic proteins ACR-2, CAM-1, and FBN-1 accumulate within the cell body and largely disappear from the dendrite.
source: In unc-116(e2310) animals, however, these dendritic proteins accumulate within the cell body and largely disappear from the dendrite, suggesting that unc-116 is required for dendritic localization of postsynaptic proteins (Figure 4).
evidence: This is an experimental observation stated in the text and shown in Figure 4.

claim: unc-116 is required for dendritic localization of postsynaptic proteins.
source: In unc-116(e2310) animals, however, these dendritic proteins accumulate within the cell body and largely disappear from the dendrite, suggesting that unc-116 is required for dendritic localization of postsynaptic proteins (Figure 4).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that dendritic proteins fail to localize properly in unc-116 mutants.

claim: The minus-end-out microtubule organization in the dendrite is instructive for dendritic cargo transport by molecular motors.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that the minus-end-out MT organization in the dendrite is instructive for dendritic cargo transport by molecular motors.
evidence: This is concluded from the observations of cargo mislocalization in unc-116 mutants.

claim: Dendritic microtubule polarity discourages the plus-end motor, UNC-104, from entering and accumulating in the dendrite.
source: It discourages the plus-end motor, UNC-104, and encourage the minus-end motor, dynein, from entering and accumulating in the dendrite.
evidence: This is inferred from the localization patterns of motors in wild-type versus unc-116 mutants.

claim: Dendritic microtubule polarity encourages the minus-end motor, dynein, to enter and accumulate in the dendrite.
source: It discourages the plus-end motor, UNC-104, and encourage the minus-end motor, dynein, from entering and accumulating in the dendrite.
evidence: This is inferred from the localization patterns of motors in wild-type versus unc-116 mutants.

claim: The microtubule polarity mechanism is essential for setting up the polarized distribution of vital axonal and dendritic constituents such as synaptic vesicles and neurotransmitter receptors.
source: This polarity mechanism is thus essential for setting up the polarized distribution of vital axonal and dendritic constituents such as SVs and neurotransmitter receptors.
evidence: This is concluded from the observations that both axonal and dendritic proteins mislocalize when MT polarity is disrupted.

claim: Kinesin-1 is composed of an N-terminal motor domain, a putative coiled-coil dimerization stalk region, and a C-terminal tail domain that binds to kinesin light chains (KLCs), adaptors, and cargos.
source: Like kinesin-1, UNC-116 is composed of an N-terminal motor domain, a putative coiled-coil dimerization stalk region, and a C-terminal tail domain that binds to kinesin light chains (KLCs), adaptors, and cargos (Vale, 2003).
evidence: This is stated as known information about kinesin-1 structure with a citation.

claim: Part of the C-terminal tail domain of kinesin-1 binds directly to microtubules.
source: Interestingly, several recent biochemical and cell biology experiments have shown that part of the C-terminal tail domain of kinesin-1 binds directly to MTs (Navone et al., 1992; Dietrich et al., 2008; Seeger and Rice, 2010).
evidence: This is stated as known information from recent studies with citations.

claim: Kinesin-1 could cross-link and glide microtubules in vitro.
source: It was also demonstrated that kinesin-1 could cross-link and glide MTs using in vitro assays (Andrews et al., 1993; Palacios and St Johnston, 2002; Yamada et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as known information from in vitro studies with citations.

claim: When purified tubulins were polymerized into microtubules, the microtubules were found as isolated microtubules with the appearance of smooth surface under the electron microscope.
source: When purified tubulins were polymerized into MTs, the MTs were found as isolated microtubules with the appearance of smooth surface under the electron microscope (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation stated in the text and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Addition of purified kinesin-1 complex from bovine brain to the microtubules causes the dispersed microtubules to adopt a more 'rough' surface due to the binding of kinesin-1 to microtubules.
source: Addition of purified kinesin-1 complex from bovine brain to the MTs causes the dispersed MTs to adopt a more 'rough' surface due to the binding of kinesin-1 to MTs (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation stated in the text and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: When both kinesin-1 and mNUDC were added to the microtubules, microtubules were bundled.
source: When both of kinesin-1 and mNUDC were added to the MTs, we found that MTs were bundled (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation stated in the text and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: No microtubule bundles were observed in control samples containing just taxol-stabilized microtubules.
source: No such bundles were observed in control samples containing just taxol-stabilized MTs or in mixtures of MTs with kinesin-1 only (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation stated in the text and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: No microtubule bundles were observed in mixtures of microtubules with kinesin-1 only.
source: No such bundles were observed in control samples containing just taxol-stabilized MTs or in mixtures of MTs with kinesin-1 only (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation stated in the text and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Neighboring microtubules in the bundles have an interval of approximately 80 nm.
source: Neighboring MTs in the bundles has an interval of ∼80 nm.
evidence: This is a measurement from the electron microscopy images.

claim: Kinesin-1 has a long flexible stalk with a maximum length of approximately 80 nm.
source: Considering kinesin-1 has a long flexible stalk (maximum ∼80 nm; Hirokawa et al., 1989) and mNUDC is an adapter protein, it is conceivable that the cross-bridges represent a complex of kinesin-1 and mNUDC.
evidence: This is stated as known information with a citation.

claim: The cross-bridges between microtubules represent a complex of kinesin-1 and mNUDC.
source: Considering kinesin-1 has a long flexible stalk (maximum ∼80 nm; Hirokawa et al., 1989) and mNUDC is an adapter protein, it is conceivable that the cross-bridges represent a complex of kinesin-1 and mNUDC.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural properties of kinesin-1 and the spacing of microtubules in bundles.

claim: Nine pairs (69%) of microtubule bundles were anti-parallel with a 95% confidence interval of 39% and 91%.
source: Nine pairs (69%) of microtubule bundles were anti-parallel with a 95% confidence interval (CI) of 39% and 91% by F-test for binominal distribution (Figure 5D-D2).
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of the polarity of cross-linked microtubules stated in the text and shown in Figure 5D-D2.

claim: Kinesin-1-mNUDC complex tends to cross-link anti-parallel microtubule bundles.
source: Therefore, kinesin-1-mNUDC complex tends to cross-link anti-parallel microtubule bundles.
evidence: This is concluded from the statistical analysis showing a significant preference for anti-parallel orientation.

claim: The C-terminal domain of kinesin-1 has been shown to bind to microtubules in addition to the N-terminal motor domain.
source: Indeed, the C-terminal domain of kinesin-1 has been shown to bind to MTs in addition to the N-terminal motor domain (Navone et al., 1992; Seeger and Rice, 2010).
evidence: This is stated as known information with citations.

claim: The MT-binding site in the C-terminal region of UNC-116 is highly conserved across species.
source: Sequence alignment of UNC-116 with its corresponding fly, rat, and human homologs showed that the MT-binding site is highly conserved (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is an observation from sequence alignment analysis stated in the text and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The positively charged residues in the C-terminal MT-binding region have been shown to be required for MT-binding in vitro.
source: The positively charged residues (labeled in red) in this region have been shown to be required for MT-binding in vitro (Seeger and Rice, 2010).
evidence: This is stated as known information with a citation.

claim: GFP-tagged C-terminal domain of UNC-116 (521–863) showed colocalization with microtubules when expressed in HEK293 cells.
source: Furthermore, GFP-tagged C-terminal domain of UNC-116 (521–863) showed colocalization with MTs when expressed in HEK293 cells, suggesting that the C-terminal domain of UNC-116 can indeed bind to MTs (data not shown).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from cell culture experiments.

claim: The C-terminal domain of UNC-116 can bind to microtubules.
source: Furthermore, GFP-tagged C-terminal domain of UNC-116 (521–863) showed colocalization with MTs when expressed in HEK293 cells, suggesting that the C-terminal domain of UNC-116 can indeed bind to MTs (data not shown).
evidence: This is inferred from the colocalization experiment in HEK293 cells.

claim: The molecular lesion of e2310 is a TC5 transposon insertion.
source: The molecular lesion of e2310 is a TC5 transposon insertion.
evidence: This is stated as known information about the e2310 allele.

claim: The transposon in e2310 was inserted after residue 692, which truncates the C-terminal MT-binding domain.
